Session 1 — Plausibility is not verification

Today’s Case — The convincing citation
You receive an LLM-generated answer containing several citations.
Before searching, classify each citation:

likely real;
suspicious;
impossible to judge from appearance.



Predict
How confident are you that a realistic journal title, DOI, court citation, or author list is genuine?
Record 0–100.


Encounter — Hallucination taxonomy
We will distinguish at least four failure types:
Fabrication
The source or fact does not exist.
Unsupported claim
The claim may be possible, but no adequate evidence is supplied.
Source distortion
The source exists but does not support the claim attributed to it.
Inference inflation
Evidence supports a narrower statement than the model presents.


Probe — Citation verification ladder
For each citation:

Existence → Identity → Source access → Claim match → Independent corroboration when needed

A search result snippet is not the final verification step.

title: Week 6 — When Algorithms Decide About People
text:
Session 1 — Same accuracy, different errors

Today’s Case — COMPAS
ProPublica examined risk scores assigned to defendants in Broward County, Florida and compared the scores with later arrests.
The central problem was not simply:

“the system makes errors”

but:

the errors were distributed differently across groups.



Predict
Before seeing the table, answer:

If two groups have approximately similar overall accuracy, must the system be equally fair to both groups?

Yes / No / Unsure
Explain why.


Encounter — Error patterns
Using the instructor-provided simplified table, identify:

true positive;
false positive;
true negative;
false negative.

Then compare group-specific error rates.


Probe — Change the fairness definition
Evaluate the same system from several perspectives:
Predictive performance
Does a high score mean something similar across groups?
False-positive parity
Are non-events incorrectly flagged at similar rates?
False-negative parity
Are events incorrectly missed at similar rates?
Overall accuracy
Is total correct classification similar?


Explain — Fairness is a choice of criterion
The class confronts:

A model can satisfy one fairness criterion while violating another.

The question therefore becomes partly normative:

Which error matters in this decision context, to whom, and why?

title: Week 6 — When Algorithms Decide About People
text:
Session 2 — Counterfactual probing

Synthetic decision case
You will receive a fictional hiring, lending, scholarship, or public-service profile.
The system makes a recommendation.
Change one attribute at a time.
Possible variables:

years of experience;
employment gap;
postcode;
institution;
income history;
age;
another instructor-approved feature.



Probe
For each changed variable ask:

Is this feature directly relevant?
Is it a plausible proxy for something else?
Would using this feature require justification?
Does one changed output prove systematic discrimination?



Inference rule
A counterfactual probe can reveal sensitivity.
One example does not establish population-level discrimination.

title: Week 4 — What Does an LLM Actually Do?
text:
Session 2 — Training, generation, retrieval

Three processes students often mix together
Training
Model parameters are adjusted using large amounts of data.
Generation / inference
A trained model produces outputs from the current input and context.
Retrieval / tool use
A surrounding system may search the web, query a database, use memory, call a calculator, or access files.






WarningCritical distinction



A chat assistant that can browse the web is not evidence that the underlying language model “stored the whole web” or “looked up the answer from its training data.”
Tool use changes the system.




Probe — Controlled model variation
Use one non-time-sensitive prompt.
Run it:

in three fresh sessions; or
under three controlled prompt conditions.

Change one variable at a time.
Record what changed, what remained stable, what you can infer, and what you cannot infer.


Explain — Variability is information
Do not conclude:

“The model is random, so nothing can be trusted.”

Instead ask:

Which aspects are stable enough to use, and which require verification?

title: Week 2 — Who Decides What You See?
text:
Session 1 — Visibility is not neutral

Today’s Case — Same need, different information environment
You will receive one information need.
Before searching, predict:

what the first three results are likely to look like;
which sources you expect to dominate;
whether two systems should show essentially the same information.



Predict
Record:

expected overlap between two systems: 0–100%;
expected overlap between two differently worded queries: 0–100%;
one reason results might differ.



Encounter — Ranking audit
Run the same information need using:

Query A: neutral/descriptive wording;
Query B: meaningfully different framing;
System 1: one search environment;
System 2: a second search environment available in the lab.

Capture the top five results for each condition.


Probe — What changed?
Compare result overlap, source types, ordering, sponsored content, recency, viewpoint diversity, and snippets/headlines.






WarningInference rule



Different rankings demonstrate different visibility conditions.
They do not, by themselves, prove manipulation, persuasion, or discriminatory intent.

title: Week 2 — Who Decides What You See?
text:
Session 2 — From targeting to persuasion

Case Ladder — Cambridge Analytica
For each step classify the evidence as:
Established / Plausible but incomplete / Requires stronger causal evidence

User data were collected.
Profiles were constructed.
Audiences could be targeted.
Targeted users were exposed to messages.
Exposure changed attitudes.
Changed attitudes altered voting behaviour.

The objective is not to defend or dismiss Cambridge Analytica. It is to identify where the evidence burden changes.


Explain — Targeting capability is not behavioural effect
Discuss:

If a platform can target people precisely, does that demonstrate that the messages are persuasive?

Separate capability evidence from effect evidence.


Troll farms and computational propaganda
Identify automation, coordination, amplification, imitation of consensus, and potential exposure.
Then ask:

What evidence would we need to claim that this campaign changed attitudes or votes?



Evidence check — Exposure is not effect
The instructor introduces empirical evidence on exposure to the Russian Internet Research Agency campaign.
Compare:

large-scale operation
with
measured relationship with attitude or voting change

The methodological lesson is:

An influence attempt can be real even when behavioural effect is uncertain, small, concentrated, or difficult to identify.

Session 3 — When can we say “the algorithm influenced me”?

Pair Challenge — Influence Claim Audit
Each pair receives one statement such as:

“The algorithm radicalised users.”
“This campaign changed the election.”
“Personalisation trapped users in a bubble.”
“The recommender made this product go viral.”

Produce:

the exact claim;
evidence for the mechanism;
evidence for exposure;
evidence for outcome;
the strongest inference you can responsibly make.



Decide
Choose one:

Mechanism established; effect unknown
Exposure established; effect unknown
Effect evidence present but limited
Claim supported within stated scope
Claim overstates available evidence



Verify
Ask:

What evidence independent of the platform, campaign, or claimant supports this judgment?

Type: Multiple choice

Which statement best distinguishes a claim from evidence?

C. Claims are subjective; evidence is always objective.
D. A claim becomes evidence when many websites repeat it.

Type: Multiple choice

You find the same statistic on eight news websites. All eight cite the same unnamed “recent study.” What is the strongest next step?

COMPLETE

Authentic original artifact is identifiable.
Three meaningfully different queries are shown.

no traceable search process;
only opinion or generated prose submitted;
evidence links absent without explanation.

Ranking, recommendation, targeting, computational propaganda, and the distinction between exposure and effect.

Phase II — Understand and Stress-Test AI
Weeks 4–6
The second phase moves from identifying AI systems to understanding and testing their behaviour.

Week 4 — What Does an LLM Actually Do?
Tokens, prediction, attention, context, generation, retrieval, and controlled variation.
Week 5 — Can AI Make You Better?
Capability boundaries, benchmark interpretation, skill boosting, and verification cost.
Week 6 — When Algorithms Decide About People
Risk scores, false positives, false negatives, fairness metrics, and counterfactual probing.

Weeks 8–11
The third phase develops increasingly deliberate control over LLM-assisted work.

Week 8 — Prompt Design Studio
Task specification, context, constraints, evidence requirements, and iterative prompting.
Week 9 — Context Drift
Context-window capacity, context utilisation, irrelevant and conflicting context, and strategic resets.
Week 10 — Hallucination Hunt

Week 11 — Academic Integrity and AI-Use Judgment

The final phase shifts from competent use toward governance, accountability, and transfer.

Week 12 — Context-Specific AI Guidelines
Risk profiles, professional rules, verification thresholds, and Final Project Gate 1.
Week 13 — Professional Accountability and Design Freeze
Human oversight, automation bias, decision rights, stop conditions, and Final Project Gate 2.
Week 14 — TRACE Transfer and Final Readiness
Transfer to unfamiliar problems, evidence auditing, and final readiness.

title: Week 1 — How Do You Know?
text:
TipThis week’s central question



How do you know that something you see online is true?
This week is not simply about “finding the correct news story.” The deeper goal is to make visible why we trust a claim, what evidence changes our judgment, and how we trace information back to inspectable evidence.

title: Week 1 — How Do You Know?
text:
TRACE this week

Predict → Encounter → Probe → Explain → Decide → Verify

TRACE is not an answer formula. It is a working protocol for keeping epistemic control with you when you encounter a claim, search result, algorithmic decision, or LLM output.

title: Week 1 — How Do You Know?

text:
Before class
This section must be completed before class.

1. Watch — How to choose your news
Damon Brown, TED-Ed — approximately 4.5 minutes.
Watch: How to choose your news
While watching, keep one question in mind:

What does the fact that a news item reached you actually tell you about whether it is true?



2. Read — Teyit methodology
Read the current Teyit methodology page, focusing especially on:

how claims are scanned and identified;
how claims are selected and prioritised;
how evidence and sources are made traceable.

title: Week 1 — How Do You Know?
text:
Session 1 — From impression to investigation

1. Today’s Case — The claim arrives first
At the beginning of class, you will be shown a claim taken from a real digital environment.
Do not search yet.
First, record the following individually:

Probability that the claim is correct: 0–100
Initial judgment: Trust / Doubt / Unsure
The single strongest signal behind that judgment







WarningTRACE rule



Record your prediction before seeing the evidence. Saying “I already thought that” after the result is known is not evidence of learning.




2. Predict
Complete this sentence in one minute:

“At this point, I am ___% confident in this claim because …”

Then compare only your reasoning with the person next to you. Do not yet argue about who is correct.


3. Encounter
Now inspect the page, post, or artifact containing the claim in full.
Record:

Who is making the claim?
Where was it published?
Is there a date?
Is a source cited?
If there is a link, does it lead to the original source or merely to another report?
Is the claim specific enough to be tested?



4. Probe I — Search differently
Investigate the same claim using at least three meaningfully different search strategies.
Query A — Exact phrase
Search a distinctive part of the claim in quotation marks.
Query B — Source-oriented
Search for the institution, researcher, report, dataset, or document supposedly behind the claim.
Query C — Evidence-oriented
Search for the data, report, study, primary document, or official record that could actually test the claim—not merely another page repeating it.
Do not stop at the first search result.


5. Skill Studio — Source tracing
Try to reconstruct this chain:

Claim → Publisher → Cited source → Original source → Independent evidence

If a link in the chain cannot be found, record that as a result. “I could not find it” can be an important finding when the missing link should exist.


6. Probe II — Leave the page
Do not evaluate an unfamiliar source only through its own self-description.
Open new tabs and investigate:

What do independent sources say about the publisher or author?
How is the same claim reported elsewhere?
Is there an earlier or more original version?
Are apparently different reports actually independent, or are they all repeating the same source?



7. Explain — What changed?
Short class discussion:

What signal influenced your initial trust judgment most strongly?
Which query produced the most useful result?
Did many repeated reports actually represent many independent pieces of evidence?
Did the claim change when you reached the primary or original source?

title: Week 1 — How Do You Know?
section: Session 2 — From investigation to defensible judgment
text:
Session 2 — From investigation to defensible judgment

8. Pair Challenge — Trace before you trust
Work in pairs on a second claim.
Each pair must produce four outputs:

One-sentence claim — What exactly is being claimed?
Best query — Which search query was most productive?
Strongest evidence — What is the strongest evidence you found?
Rejected result — Give one result you deliberately did not use and explain why.

When groups compare results, compare not only the verdicts but also the search paths that produced them.


9. Decide — Make a defensible judgment
Classify the claim using one of the following categories:

Supported — Available evidence supports the claim.
Contradicted — Credible evidence conflicts with the claim.
Unsupported — There is not enough evidence to support the claim.
Missing context — Part of the claim may be correct, but missing context materially changes its meaning.
Unresolved — The available public evidence does not support a reliable conclusion.

Defend your judgment in two sentences.


10. Verify — Independent evidence
Before closing the case, ask:

What evidence independent of the original claimant supports my final judgment?

If you cannot find independent evidence, recalibrate your confidence accordingly.


11. Recalibrate
Return to your initial confidence score.

Initial confidence: ___ / 100
Final confidence: ___ / 100
Change: ___

The key question is not simply “Was my first guess correct?”

Did my judgment change as much as the evidence warranted?

Predictive AI and generative AI
Compare:

“AI is all fake.”

Four context problems
Irrelevant context
Information that is present but not useful.
Stale context
Earlier assumptions that are no longer valid.

Instructions or facts that point in different directions.

Information required for a defensible answer but never supplied.


Context Brief
Build a compact state record:

Goal → Known facts → Constraints → Decisions already made → Open questions → Evidence standard

Use the brief to start a fresh session.
